summary: Defines the X.509 certificate profile used to show who holds the right to use Internet number resources. It is the normative description of certificate and revocation list syntax in the RPKI. It was later updated by RFC 7318, RFC 8209 and RFC 9829.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6487 sets strict rules for certificates that list which Internet addresses and network numbers an organization may use. It also explains how systems check those certificates and learn when an issuer has revoked one.

questions: what is in an rpki certificate
what is an rpki resource certificate
subtitle: The certificate and revocation-list rules used to represent Internet number resources in the RPKI.

tldr.problem: The Resource Public Key Infrastructure needs certificates that consistently state which IP addresses and Autonomous System numbers an issuer has authorized a subject to use.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6487 narrows the X.509 certificate and CRL formats, defines resource extensions and certificate request profiles, and specifies how a relying party validates a certificate path and its resource ranges.
tldr.outcome: It defines certificate and CRL syntax for the RPKI and was later updated by RFC 7318, RFC 8209, and RFC 9829.

today: RFC 6487 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7318, RFC 8209, and RFC 9829. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What a Resource Certificate Represents
sections.content:
A resource certificate is an X.509 certificate that states an issuer has granted its subject a right of use for listed Internet Number Resources (INRs): IP addresses, Autonomous System (AS) numbers, or both. RFC 6487 defines the RPKI profile for these certificates, certificate revocation lists (CRLs), certificate requests, and relying-party path validation.

The profile requires listed fields and forbids extensions that it does not explicitly permit. A certificate authority (CA) following the RPKI Certificate Policy MUST issue certificates and CRLs that follow these rules.
sections.plainLanguage: A resource certificate links a public key to the IP addresses or AS numbers that an issuer has authorized its holder to use. RFC 6487 defines the exact certificate format and how to check it.

sections.title: Resource Ranges and End-Entity Certificates
sections.content:
Each resource certificate MUST contain an IP Address Delegation extension, an AS Identifier Delegation extension, or both. These extensions MUST be critical and use the canonical resource format defined by RFC 3779, except when the certificate uses the inherit form. During validation, an issuer's resources must be the same as or a superset of the subject's resources.

An end-entity (EE) certificate is used to verify a signed RPKI object, such as a Route Origin Authorization or manifest. Its private key normally signs one object, and revoking that certificate effectively revokes the object. The RFC also defines sequential-use certificates for a sequence of objects that replace one another at the same publication point.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate can list only resources that its issuer also covers. An end-entity certificate links a signing key to an RPKI object, so revoking the certificate also revokes that object.

sections.title: Required Certificate Fields and Extensions
sections.content:
Unless the profile marks a field optional, it MUST appear, and fields not listed by the profile MUST NOT appear. Resource certificates use X.509 version 3, a positive serial number unique for each issuing CA, and the signature and public-key algorithms specified by RFC 6485. Issuer and subject names have constrained distinguished-name formats; the issuer chooses the subject name.

The profile also sets detailed extension rules. For example, the Subject Key Identifier is required and uses a 160-bit SHA-1 hash, while Key Usage differs for CA and EE certificates. Resource extensions are critical. A CA certificate must include Basic Constraints, while an EE certificate must not.

Authority, distribution, and subject information extensions point to issuer certificates, revocation lists, repositories, manifests, or signed objects as appropriate to the certificate role. The profile prefers rsync URIs for these references.
sections.plainLanguage: Every resource certificate has a fixed set of fields, and extra unapproved extensions are not allowed. The rules differ for CA certificates and end-entity certificates because they have different jobs.

sections.title: Revocation Lists and Certificate Requests
sections.content:
Each CA MUST issue a version 2 CRL covering all certificates it issued. A CRL MUST include its Authority Key Identifier and CRL Number, and it MUST NOT use indirect or delta CRLs. If a CA issues more than one CRL, the one with the highest CRL Number supersedes the others. A revoked-certificate entry contains only its serial number and revocation date.

A certificate request may use PKCS#10 or CRMF. A CA MUST support PKCS#10 and MAY support CRMF. The CA may change most requested fields when issuing a certificate, but it must honor a conforming Subject Information Access request or reject the request. The profile does not define a certificate response message.
sections.plainLanguage: A CA publishes a revocation list for all its certificates, and the list identifies revoked certificates by serial number. A requester can send a PKCS#10 request; the issuer sets most certificate details.

sections.title: How Relying Parties Validate a Path
sections.content:
A relying party validates a chain from a trust anchor to the target certificate. Each certificate's subject must match the next certificate's issuer, and each signature must verify with the issuer's public key. The current time must fall within each certificate's validity period.

The relying party checks that every required field is present, forbidden fields are absent, and the certificate is not on the issuer's valid current CRL. The key that verifies the CRL must be the same key that verifies the certificate. At every step, the issuer's resource set must encompass the next certificate's resources, beginning with the trust anchor's resources.

Implementations may stop validation when a path exceeds a locally configured length limit. This can help avoid spending unlimited effort on very long or looping paths.
sections.plainLanguage: To check a certificate, follow its issuers up to a trust anchor. At each step, check signatures, dates, revocation status, required fields, and that the listed resources fit within the issuer's resources.

sections.title: Coordinating a Future Profile Change
sections.content:
Relying parties must reject certificates and CRLs that do not conform to the profile. This means changing the profile is not backward compatible, so CAs and relying parties must coordinate the change. The RFC describes a three-phase transition for a future profile update.

First, all CAs become able to issue certificates under the new profile when requested. Next, CAs issue both old and new formats while relying parties may accept either. Finally, all relying parties must support the new format and CAs issue only that format. At the end, the old format is removed.
sections.plainLanguage: A profile change requires coordinated updates because systems reject certificates that do not match the rules. The RFC describes a staged move from the old format to the new one, with a period when both formats coexist.

sections.title: Security Limits of the Profile
sections.content:
The security guidance for X.509 certificates, resource extensions, and certificate requests also applies here. The RPKI certificate system cannot resolve a conflict when valid certificates claim the same resource; if issuance reflects allocation records, the certificate is only as reliable as those records.

The profile requires the same key to sign a certificate and the CRL that can revoke it. A relying-party implementation that builds separate validation paths for the certificate and its CRL can create a risk, especially if subject names collide and the implementation does not follow this profile.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate cannot fix an incorrect or conflicting resource allocation record. The same issuer key must validate both a certificate and the list that can revoke it.

viz.caption: THE PROFILE CHANGE USES THREE TRANSITION PHASES

items.title: Phase 1
items.text: CAs can issue under the new profile when requested.

items.title: Phase 2
items.text: CAs issue both formats; relying parties may use either.

items.title: Phase 3
items.text: Relying parties support the new format and CAs issue only it.
